title: Does the EU Cyber Resilience Act require manufacturers to train their staff?
description: What Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 means for manufacturer staff skills: no training article, 24 hour reporting since September 2026, full rules in December 2027.
shortAnswer: No. The EU Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, contains no article requiring manufacturers to train employees. Recital 23 says manufacturers should ensure their staff have the skills needed to comply, and the operative duties make that unavoidable: vulnerability reporting within 24 hours has applied since September 11, 2026, and secure by design and vulnerability handling requirements apply from December 11, 2027.
keyTakeaways: There is no explicit staff training obligation for manufacturers; the closest text is recital 23, which is not binding on its own.
Article 14 reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents has applied since September 11, 2026, including to products already on the market.
The rest of the Regulation applies from December 11, 2027; rules on notifying conformity assessment bodies applied from June 11, 2026.
Breaches of Annex I or Articles 13 and 14 can draw fines of up to EUR 15 million or 2.5% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
Articles 10 and 33 place skills and training duties on Member States, including awareness and training activities for micro and small enterprises.
regulator: National market surveillance authorities in each Member State; European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and designated CSIRTs for reporting; European Commission
appliesTo: Manufacturers of products with digital elements made available on the EU market, including software and connected hardware
Importers and distributors of those products
Product security, engineering, PSIRT and incident response staff who carry out the manufacturer's obligations

sections.heading: Is there an explicit training requirement in the CRA?

blocks.text: No article of the [Cyber Resilience Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202402847) obliges manufacturers to train staff, set competence criteria or keep training records. That distinguishes it from instruments such as the [EU AI Act's AI literacy article](/regulations/eu-ai-act-ai-literacy) or [NIS2's management body training duty](/regulations/nis2-management-body-training).

The only manufacturer focused statement on skills is in recital 23. After calling on Member States to ensure tasks are carried out by adequately trained professionals, it says: "Similarly, manufacturers should ensure that their staff has the necessary skills to comply with their obligations as laid down in this Regulation." Recitals explain the purpose of the operative text but do not create freestanding obligations.

Training duties in the operative text fall on Member States. Article 10 requires them to promote measures to develop cybersecurity skills, including "re-skilling or up-skilling for manufacturers' employees." Article 33(1)(a) requires them, where appropriate, to organize specific awareness raising and training activities about the Regulation for micro and small enterprises.

sections.heading: When do the CRA obligations apply?

blocks.text: The CRA applies in three stages under Article 71, and the first manufacturer obligation is already live. EUR-Lex lists entry into force on December 10, 2024, after publication in the Official Journal on November 20, 2024.

blocks.text: Article 69(3) extends the Article 14 reporting duty to all in scope products placed on the market before December 11, 2027. A manufacturer cannot defer reporting readiness on the ground that a product predates the Regulation. As at November 2026, EUR-Lex records amendments to Article 13(4) and related provisions by the European Health Data Space Regulation (EU) 2025/327, applying from March 26, 2027, and two Commission delegated regulations, but no change to the Article 71 dates.

sections.heading: What do the reporting deadlines demand of staff?

blocks.text: Article 14 sets clocks that start when the manufacturer becomes aware, so the people who first see a report must recognize it and escalate it at once. For an actively exploited vulnerability the manufacturer must notify the CSIRT designated as coordinator and ENISA, through the single reporting platform, with:

items: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware;
a vulnerability notification within 72 hours, with general information, the nature of the exploit and corrective or mitigating measures;
a final report no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available.

blocks.text: Severe incidents follow the same 24 hour and 72 hour steps, with a final report within one month of the incident notification. Article 14(8) also requires the manufacturer to inform impacted users, and where appropriate all users, about the vulnerability or incident and mitigations.

Meeting these deadlines depends on decisions made by individuals under time pressure: is this vulnerability actively exploited, is this incident severe, which Member States are affected, how sensitive is the information. Those judgments are competencies that can be defined, trained and assessed, and exercised through scenario drills. The organizations most at risk are those where customer support or community managers receive reports but do not know what "actively exploited" means for the clock.

sections.heading: Which December 2027 obligations depend on skilled staff?

blocks.text: From December 11, 2027, manufacturers must design, develop and produce products in line with the essential cybersecurity requirements in Annex I Part I (Article 13(1)) and must assess and document cybersecurity risks across planning, design, development, production, delivery and maintenance (Article 13(2) and (3)). These are engineering practices, so the competence sits with product and development teams.
Annex I Part II sets vulnerability handling duties that require specific know how, including:

items: drawing up a software bill of materials covering at least top level dependencies;
addressing and remediating vulnerabilities without delay, including through security updates provided separately from functionality updates where technically feasible;
applying effective and regular tests and reviews of product security;
publicly disclosing fixed vulnerabilities once an update is available;
putting in place and enforcing a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy, with a contact address for reports.

sections.heading: What penalties apply if staff get it wrong?

blocks.text: Article 64 links the heaviest fines to the obligations that most depend on staff competence. Non compliance with the essential cybersecurity requirements in Annex I and the obligations in Articles 13 and 14 can draw administrative fines of up to EUR 15,000,000 or, for an undertaking, up to 2.5% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.

Lower tiers apply to other obligations: up to EUR 10,000,000 or 2% for a listed set of provisions including importer and distributor duties, and up to EUR 5,000,000 or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies and market surveillance authorities. Member States set the detailed penalty rules. Trained staff reduce the chance of a missed 24 hour window and of inaccurate statements to authorities.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Because the CRA states outcomes rather than training rules, Knowledge Foundry starts from the obligations, such as Article 14 deadlines and Annex I Part II duties, and derives the competencies and assessment points each role needs. The resulting map shows which people can make a reporting decision and evidences readiness without inventing a legal training requirement.

faqs.a: No. Recitals explain the reasons for the operative provisions and can guide interpretation, but they do not impose obligations by themselves. Recital 23 signals that the legislator expects manufacturers' staff to have the skills to comply, so a lack of skills is unlikely to be accepted as an explanation for a missed reporting deadline.

faqs.q: Do the reporting obligations apply to software already on sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Article 69(3) applies the Article 14 reporting obligations to all products with digital elements within scope that were placed on the market before December 11, 2027. Manufacturers therefore needed reporting procedures and trained staff in place by September 11, 2026 for their existing portfolio.

faqs.q: Who counts as a manufacturer under the CRA?
faqs.a: Article 3 defines a manufacturer as a natural or legal person who develops or manufactures products with digital elements, or has them designed, developed or manufactured, and markets them under its name or trademark, whether for payment, monetization or free of charge. Software publishers selling into the EU are typically manufacturers.

faqs.q: How does the CRA relate to NIS2 training duties?
faqs.a: They cover different subjects. NIS2 regulates essential and important entities and requires management body cybersecurity training. The CRA regulates products and places obligations on manufacturers, importers and distributors. A software company can be subject to both and should map each obligation separately, using shared competencies where they overlap.
